text_to_speech: You remember when Boston Dynamics  published a video of Atlas, where it   did [funny squeaking], and then [funny squeaking]  and then we were all like [crowd going wow ]. And   then a wise man, who did not own Twitter at the  time, said "This is nothing. In a few years, that   bot will move so fast, you'll need a strobe light  to see it. Sweet dreams". Well, I'm still waiting   for my atomic car and my hoverboard. However,  the progress in robotics locomotion in the last   few years has been nothing short of amazing.  Today, I want to talk to you about how robots   can imitate the motion of humans or animals. I  know it can get a bit technical at times, but   believe me by the end of this 8-minute video, you  will have a really good idea of how this works. In one of my previous videos, I used reinforcement  learning to teach a robotic dog, Beetle, how to   move forward, left, and right. There, I used a  handcrafted reward function, which incentivizes   the behavior you want the robot to do, in this  case, walking, and penalizes everything else the   robot might be doing, such as flying, walking  on its knees, standing on its head, jumping.   Creating an accurate, stable reward function is  really challenging. The robot may exhibit some   strange behaviors, as I mentioned earlier. The  primary component of a reward function is the   difference between the random commands we give to  the robot and the actual velocity of the robot.   For example, we give a command to move forward at  a speed of 1 meter per second, and then we measure   the robot's actual velocity. The difference  between them is the reward or punishment. But   having only this primary component is not enough;  it's too crude and leads to all sorts of unwanted   behavior. So we add more things to the reward  function: feet-ground time, whether the joints   are at their maximum positions, the termination  reward or punishment if the robot doesn't last   until the end of the round in the simulation, and  so on. This fine-tuning of the reward function   can be really time-consuming, even with Isaac  Gym, which speeds up things considerably. But   you'll need around 10-20 minutes to see  the results and repeat this many times. Walking is not rocket science; it's  about putting your left foot forward,   then your right, and off you go. So we don't want  the robot to figure out walking from scratch. We   can tell the robot approximately what walking is  like and then make sure it can apply it to its   particular structure. This concept is not super  complicated. Some smart people wrote papers on   the topic. They had an idea that you can teach  locomotion by providing a hint to the policy,   the robot, in the form of motion capture files.  This is where so-called adversarial motion priors   come into play. In the paper, which is quite  interesting and has a few visual demos, there are   two reward components: a discriminator reward and  a task reward. The task reward is pretty simple,   like moving in a certain direction or to a  specific location. The second component is the   discriminator reward. When combined, the goal of  the policy is to complete the task while imitating   the style of movement from the motion capture  files. The motion files were taken from Carnegie   Mellon University's motion capture library and  include movements like walking, running, jumping,   yoga poses, etc. There's no need for direct  correlation between the tasks and the motion   capture files because the discriminator evaluates  how closely the policy's movement resembles the   one from the motion capture files. Over time,  the policy will hopefully become similar in style   to the motion capture file's movement and also  complete the given task. This approach is similar   to generative adversarial networks or GANs,  which were all the rage for generating images   before Stable Diffusion was introduced. This  approach works well for robotic movements too. The powerful thing about adversarial motion  priors is that in motion capture files,   you only have observations; you don't  know at what angle or position the   joint was to complete the action. But  with the adversarial motion priors,   you don't need that information because the  discriminator only judges the observations   and has nothing to do with the actions.  After my video about Beetle, I thought about   how beneficial it would be for the policy to have  access to hints in the form of animal movements,   as it was a quadruped robot. Time passed, and  I forgot about it. But recently, while looking   at Isaac Gym environment's repository, I found  they implemented the adversarial motion prior   example from the paper. They implemented the  style component but not the task component,   which was quite easy to add. Researchers from ETH  Zurich implemented adversarial motion priors for   a wheeled version of an animal robot, and it  worked fantastically for them. I decided to   give it a shot and try implementing it with Boston  Dynamics' Atlas. I know it's not very likely that   I'll be able to try out what I have on a real  robot, but who knows? Robert, call me, maybe. What I did was take the motion files for a human  because Atlas is a humanoid robot, and then I went   on a journey of exploration. Honestly, it was not  easy. The code that Nvidia had for this example is   good research code; it's very reproducible if you  just want to reproduce that particular experiment   with humanoid characters. But if you want to try  it with your own robots, there are a lot of RAKES   to step on. I want to give you an overview of the  steps. This is not production-ready code, but I   hope that if you follow my guide, you'll only step  on two or three RAKES instead of 200, like I did. To see the code instructions, follow onto the  next video, or if you're more interested in   large language models and how you can run a  custom GPT approximation on your computer,   then here's another playlist  about large language models.

youtube_description:
Learn how to use Deep Reinforcement Learning (a method of Machine Learning which involves rewarding the agent for doing something correctly, and punishing it for doing anything incorrectly) and Adversarial Motion Priors (Motion Imitation from Observations) for training robots lifelike movement in a simulation, with Boston Dynamics Atlas. Similar techniques are applicable to other humanoid robots, like Agility’s DIGIT used in Amazon warehouse or Tesla's Optimus - or even non-humanoid robots, such as #disney Imagineering latest adorable biped robot, currently being tested at Galaxy's Edge.

While I do not have exact information on how Boston Dynamics Atlas works, it is a good educated guess :)

Github:
https://github.com/AIWintermuteAI/IsaacGymEnvs/tree/atlas_amp_wip
Will likely merge to main branch with time.
